name: Shenqi Fuzheng injection
short: Given by injection. Allergic reactions most common, with allergic shock in serious cases; critical infusion reactions, phlebitis, low platelets reported. 51 reactions (1 severe) in 30,026 monitored.
text: Shenqi Fuzheng injection is a Chinese herbal medicine given by injection, not by mouth; a 2014 safety review describes it as a solution made of Dangshen (Radix Codonopsis) and Huangqi (Radix Astragali Mongolici). Its most serious reported harms are allergic and infusion reactions. A post-marketing safety re-evaluation, drawing on hospital monitoring, national spontaneous reports, records from 20 hospitals and the literature, found allergic reactions to be the most common adverse drug reactions, mainly involving the skin and its appendages, with systemic reactions and, in serious cases, allergic shock; reactions were more common in elderly people, which the authors say may be related to the cancer populations treated, and its early-warning analysis found a strong association between phlebitis (vein inflammation) and the injection. The authors judged its safety good overall. In a retrospective study of 505 infusion reactions to many drugs in one hospital's pharmacovigilance records, the authors list Shenqi Fuzheng among five medicines that had a higher incidence of critical infusion reactions; the abstract gives no figures for the injection. The 2014 review found 16 published case reports describing 17 cases, with symptoms including thrombocytopenia (low platelets), rash, chills, palpitations, breathlessness, swelling of a leg or the eyelids, and superficial vein inflammation. In hospital monitoring of 30,026 patients given the injection, 51 had adverse drug reactions, 1 of them severe, a rate of 1.7 per 1,000; the 2014 review reports 1.85 per 1,000 among 20,100 cases observed and 23 adverse reactions in 8,484 monitored cases. A study of records from 20 hospitals, which used dexamethasone use as a marker of a suspected allergic reaction, found such reactions associated with the single dose given and with combined use of matrine (odds ratio 14.3); this is an association in record data. In a randomized trial in 66 people with myasthenia gravis receiving methylprednisolone pulse therapy, 18.75% of the group also given the injection had slight side effects, including poor digestion and rash; the abstract gives no figure for the group given steroid pulses alone.
